regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
1. Short title and commencement
(1) These regulations may be called the International Financial Services Centres Authority
(Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025.
(2) These regulations shall come into force on and from the date of their publication in the
Official Gazette.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 1, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: This gives the rules their official name — the IFSCA (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 — and fixes when they start: the day they are published in the Official Gazette. They were notified on 11 April 2025 and published on 16 April 2025, so 16 April 2025 is the date to work from for questions about what applied when.
regulation_content.applicability: All capital market intermediaries and applicants under these regulations

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
2. Objective
These regulations provide the regulatory framework for registration, regulation and
supervision of capital market intermediaries operating in international financial services
centres in India with the objectives of protecting the interests of investors and maintaining
the integrity of the securities market.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 2, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: This states why the rules exist: to register, regulate and supervise capital market intermediaries (the licensed service providers of the market — brokers, custodians, advisers, rating agencies and the like) operating in IFSC, with two aims — protecting investors and keeping the securities market clean. It sets no duty on its own; it is the lens used to read the rest when something is unclear.
regulation_content.applicability: All capital market intermediaries and applicants under these regulations

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
3. Definitions
(1) In these regulations, unless the context otherwise requires, the terms defined herein shall
bear the meanings as assigned to them below, and their cognate expressions shall be
construed accordingly, -
(a) “Act” means the International Financial Services Centres Authority Act, 2019 (50
of 2019);
(b) “associate” in relation to a person shall include another person:
(i) who, directly or indirectly, by himself, or in combination with other persons,
exercises control over the first person;
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 3, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: This is the dictionary of the rules. It defines the terms used throughout, and anything not defined here borrows its meaning from the parent laws (the IFSCA Act, SEBI Act, Depositories Act, Companies Act and their rules). A few definitions carry real weight later: 'associate' (which pulls in anyone controlling 20% or more of voting power), 'control' (more than 50% of voting rights or the right to run the entity), 'Foreign Jurisdiction' (a country only counts if its regulator has the right international tie-ups and a clean anti-money-laundering record), and role definitions like 'principal officer' and 'compliance officer' that drive the staffing rules in Reg 9.
regulation_content.important_numbers: ‘associate’ includes control of ≥20% of voting power; ‘control’ means >50% of voting rights or interest
regulation_content.applicability: All capital market intermediaries and applicants under these regulations

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.provision_heading: Obligation to seek Registration and Exemptions therefrom
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 4, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: This is the core licensing rule: a unit in IFSC that wants to carry on any of eleven listed activities — broker dealer, clearing member, credit rating agency, custodian, debenture trustee, depository participant, distributor, ESG ratings/data provider, investment adviser, investment banker or research entity — must first get a certificate of registration from IFSCA. A firm doing several of these can now apply for a single 'unified' registration (added 12 January 2026). A Banking Unit can act as banker to an issue, or as an investment banker, on the Authority's terms. Some players are exempted — for example, an already-registered adviser, rating agency or fund manager that puts out a research report need not separately register as a research entity, and certain overseas service providers dealing with IFSC clients are outside the net (unless they set up a unit in IFSC).
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The exemptions are where most of the judgement lies. They are activity-and-status specific — an exemption for one hat (say, research) does not excuse registration for another (say, advice). The clarification is important: the moment an outside player opens a unit in IFSC to provide these services, the exemption falls away and registration is required.
regulation_content.practical_point: Map every activity the firm actually does to the eleven-item list, then check each against the exemptions before assuming a licence is or isn't needed. If the firm does more than one activity, weigh a unified registration against separate ones. Where an overseas group provides services into IFSC, watch the 'sets up a unit in IFSC' trigger.
regulation_content.example: An investment adviser already registered with IFSCA also publishes research reports to the public. It does not need a separate research-entity registration — the exemption covers it. But if the same group opens a new IFSC unit purely to sell ESG data, that unit must register as an ERDPP.
regulation_content.risk_point: The common failure is running an unregistered activity under the shelter of a registration held for a different activity, or an overseas entity providing services through an IFSC presence without registering.
regulation_content.interview_point: A firm registered as a broker dealer also wants to advise clients on their portfolios. Does it need a separate investment-adviser registration, and what exemption might apply?
regulation_content.applicability: Entities seeking a certificate of registration as a capital market intermediary in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
5. Application for registration
(1) An entity desirous of obtaining a certificate of registration as a CMI in IFSC shall
submit an application form through SWIT along with documents and application fees,
in the manner as specified by the Authority:
Provided that the applicant seeking registration to act as a broker dealer, clearing
member, depository participant shall make the application along with such additional
information through the recognised stock exchange, recognised clearing corporation,
recognised depository, as the case may be.
(2) The recognised stock exchange, the recognised clearing corporation or the
recognised depository, as the case may be, shall examine the eligibility of the applicant
in terms of these regulations, applicable Acts, rules, regulations and bye-laws, and
forward the application to the Authority along with its recommendation no later than
thirty days of receipt of the complete application.
(3) An application which is not complete in all respects shall be liable to be rejected.
(4) Subject to approval by the concerned recognised stock exchange, and without any
requirement of a separate certificate of registration, -
(a) a clearing member may be permitted to act as a broker dealer in a recognised
stock exchange; and
(b) a broker dealer may be permitted to operate in more than one recognised stock
exchange.
(5) Subject to approval by the concerned recognised clearing corporation, and without
any requirement of a separate certificate of registration, -
(a) a broker dealer may be permitted to act as a clearing member in a recognised
clearing corporation; and
(b) a clearing member may be permitted to operate in more than one recognised
clearing corporation.
(6) An entity filing an application for seeking registration as a capital market
intermediary shall comply with additional norms and requirements as may be specified
by the Authority.
(7) The provisions of these regulations, as applicable to the grant of registration shall
also apply to an application for renewal of registration of a capital market intermediary,
wherever applicable.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 5, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: This sets out how you apply. The application goes to IFSCA through SWIT (the Single Window IT System — the online registration portal) with the required documents and fee. For a broker dealer, clearing member or depository participant, the application is routed through the relevant stock exchange, clearing corporation or depository, which checks eligibility and forwards it to the Authority with its recommendation within 30 days of a complete application. An incomplete application can simply be rejected. Some cross-permissions need no fresh certificate — for example, with the exchange's approval a clearing member can also act as a broker dealer, and a broker dealer can operate on more than one exchange. The same rules apply to renewals.
regulation_content.practical_point: File a complete application on SWIT — an incomplete one can be rejected outright, resetting the timeline. For broker/clearing/DP registrations, build in the 30-day exchange/clearing/depository review step. Where you want a broker dealer to also clear, or to operate on multiple exchanges, use the cross-permission route rather than a fresh certificate.
regulation_content.risk_point: The avoidable risk is an incomplete SWIT filing that is rejected rather than queried, and mis-routing a broker/clearing/DP application directly to the Authority instead of through the market infrastructure institution.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Stock exchange / clearing corporation / depository forwards the application to the Authority within 30 days of a complete application
regulation_content.applicability: Entities seeking a certificate of registration as a capital market intermediary in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
6. Legal form of the applicant
A capital market intermediary seeking registration with the Authority shall be required to
be present in an IFSC in the form of a company or an LLP or a body corporate, or branch
thereof.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 6, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: This fixes the legal shape the applicant must take. A CMI must be present in IFSC as a company, an LLP, a body corporate, or a branch of one. So a sole proprietorship or an informal arrangement will not qualify — the entity has to have a recognised corporate form before it can be registered.
regulation_content.applicability: Entities seeking a certificate of registration as a capital market intermediary in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
7. Net worth requirements
(1) An entity seeking registration as a capital market intermediary shall comply with
the net worth requirements as specified in Schedule I of these regulations, which shall
be maintained at all times.
(2) Where a capital market intermediary is set up in the form of branch, the minimum
net worth requirements specified in these regulations may be maintained at the parent
level in the home jurisdiction where the parent entity is incorporated:
Provided that the minimum net worth maintained at the parent level shall be earmarked
for its branch in IFSC.
(3) The minimum net worth requirements under these regulations shall be separate and
in addition to the minimum net worth requirements applicable for other activities
outside IFSC or within IFSC under any other regulations or framework.
(4) Where an entity intends to operate as a capital market intermediary in multiple
categories covered under these regulations, it shall maintain the highest of the
applicable minimum net worth requirements, unless otherwise specified by the
Authority.
Explanation: Where a CMI is required to infuse capital to comply with the revised
minimum net worth requirements specified in these regulations, such entity shall ensure
compliance by October 01, 2025 or any other date as may be specified by the Authority.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 7, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Every CMI must have a minimum net worth (its own capital cushion, as defined in Reg 3) set out in Schedule I, and must keep it at all times — not just on the day it registers. A branch can hold this at its parent level abroad, but the amount must be earmarked for the IFSC branch. This IFSC net worth is separate from and on top of any net worth the firm needs for other activities. If a firm operates in several categories, it must meet the highest applicable figure. Existing CMIs that had to top up were given until 1 October 2025 to comply.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Owner: the CMI (finance function). Maintain the Schedule I net worth continuously, evidence it each quarter (see Reg 16(1)(d)), and, for a branch, keep the earmarking at parent level documented.
regulation_content.example: A firm registered as both a custodian (USD 1 million) and an investment adviser (USD 25,000) must maintain USD 1 million — the higher of the two — not the sum, and not just the adviser figure.
regulation_content.risk_point: Net worth is a continuous test: letting it dip below the Schedule I floor between reporting dates is itself a breach, even if it is topped up later.
regulation_content.interview_point: A CMI operates as a debenture trustee and a distributor. Which net-worth figure applies, and can a branch keep it at parent level?
regulation_content.important_numbers: Net worth per Schedule I, maintained at all times; where operating in multiple categories, the highest applicable net worth applies; existing CMIs to infuse capital by 01-Oct-2025
regulation_content.applicability: Entities seeking a certificate of registration as a capital market intermediary in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
8. Fit and proper requirements
(1) A capital market intermediary shall ensure that the entity and its principal officer,
directors/ designated partners, key managerial personnel and controlling shareholders
are fit and proper persons, at all times.
(2) For the purpose of sub-regulation (1), a person shall be deemed to be a fit and
proper person if, -
(a) such person has a record of fairness and integrity, including but not limited to-
(i) financial integrity;
(ii) good reputation and character; and
(iii) honesty.
(b) such person has not incurred any of the following disqualifications –
(i) the person has been convicted by a court of law for any offence involving
moral turpitude or any economic offence or any offence against securities
laws;
(ii) charge sheet has been filed against such person by any Indian enforcement
agency in matters concerning economic offences and is pending;
(iii) charges have been framed by a court of law or an equivalent institution in
matters concerning economic offences;
(iv) a recovery proceeding has been initiated against the person by a financial
regulatory authority and is pending;
(v) an order has been passed against the person for malfeasance;
(vi) the person has been declared insolvent and not discharged;
(vii) an order restraining, prohibiting or debarring the person from accessing or
dealing in financial product(s) or financial service(s), has been passed by any
regulatory authority, in any matter concerning securities laws or financial
services market and such order is in force;
(viii) any other order against the person, which has a material bearing on the
securities market, has been passed by the Authority or any other regulatory
authority, and a period of three years from the date of the order has not elapsed:
Explanation. – For the above provision, the decision to determine materiality
shall be that of the Authority;
(ix) the person has been found to be of unsound mind by a court of competent
jurisdiction and the finding is in force;
(x) the person is financially not sound or has been categorized as a wilful
defaulter;
(xi) the person has been declared a fugitive economic offender; or
(xii) any other disqualification as may be specified by the Authority.
(3) Where any person has been declared as not ‘fit and proper person’ by an order of a
regulatory authority, such a person shall not be eligible to apply for any registration,
until she satisfies the fit and proper criteria.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 8, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: The CMI, and its principal officer, directors or designated partners, key managerial personnel and controlling shareholders, must be 'fit and proper' at all times — a clean-background test of integrity and reputation. A person fails it if they carry certain disqualifications: conviction for an offence involving moral turpitude or an economic or securities offence, a pending charge sheet or framed charges in economic-offence matters, a pending recovery proceeding, a malfeasance order, undischarged insolvency, a debarment order in force, being of unsound mind, being a wilful defaulter, or being a declared fugitive economic offender. Where any other adverse order has a material bearing on the securities market, the person is disqualified until three years have passed from that order. Someone declared not fit and proper cannot apply again until they meet the test.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: 'Fit and proper' is an ongoing status, not a one-time entry gate — it must hold throughout the life of the registration, so a later conviction or debarment of a controlling shareholder can taint the CMI itself. The three-year clock applies only to the residual 'any other order with material bearing' limb; the listed disqualifications bite for as long as they subsist. Materiality of an 'other order' is the Authority's call.
regulation_content.practical_point: Screen the entity and every named person (principal officer, directors/designated partners, KMP, controlling shareholders) at application and re-test on any change or adverse development. Keep declarations and evidence current, because the test must be satisfied continuously, not only at registration.
regulation_content.risk_point: Inspections focus on whether fit-and-proper was actually re-tested after a change in directors or controllers, and whether a disqualifying event was caught and acted on rather than missed.
regulation_content.interview_point: A controlling shareholder of a CMI is later declared a wilful defaulter. What is the effect on the CMI's registration, and does the three-year clock apply?
regulation_content.important_numbers: Fit-and-proper: an adverse order with material bearing on the securities market disqualifies until 3 years from the order have elapsed
regulation_content.applicability: Entities seeking a certificate of registration as a capital market intermediary in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.provision_heading: Appointment of Principal Officer, Compliance Officer and other human resources
regulation_content.regulation_text:
9. Appointment of Principal Officer, Compliance Officer and other human resources
(1) A capital market intermediary shall designate a principal officer and a separate
compliance officer based out of IFSC.
(2) A capital market intermediary shall ensure that the principal officer and the
compliance officer meet the following educational qualification requirements:
(a) A professional qualification or post-graduate degree or post graduate diploma
(minimum one year in duration) in finance, law, accountancy, business
management, commerce, economics, capital market, banking, insurance , actuarial
science, fintech, science, technology, engineering or mathematics from a
university or an institution recognised by the Central Government or any State
Government or a 4 foreign university or institution or association or a CFA or
a FRM from Global Association of Risk Professionals or any other relevant
educational qualifications as may be specified by the Authority:
Provided that a graduation degree in any field from a university or an institution
recognised by the Central Government or any State Government or a foreign
university would suffice where the principal officer or the compliance officer has a
work experience of at least five years in the financial services market:
Provided further that a person who has a qualification of Bachelor of Law from a
university, or an institution recognised by the Central Government or any State
Government or a recognised foreign university or institution or association is also
eligible for appointment as a compliance officer:
Provided further that, in respect of a principal officer of a distributor or an
investment adviser or a research entity, a graduate degree in any field from a
university or an institution recognised by the Central Government or any State
Government or a foreign university along with a certification as a Certified
Financial Planner from Financial Planning Standards Board shall also suffice.
Explanation. - For the purposes of these regulations, the professional qualification
shall include membership of Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, Institute
of Company Secretaries of India, Institute of Cost Accountants of India or any
institution equivalent thereto in a Foreign Jurisdiction.
(3) A capital market intermediary shall ensure that the principal officer and compliance
officer meet the following experience requirements:
(a) A principal officer shall have an experience of at least three years in the financial
services market:
Provided that a person having a work experience of at least one year in ESG related
activities may also be eligible for appointment as principal officer of an ERDPP.
(b) A compliance officer shall have an experience of at least two years in the
financial services market:
Provided that the work experience in any other field shall be considered if the
person has work experience of minimum two years in compliance related role or
function in a company.
(4) The requirement of qualification and experience as mentioned in the sub-
regulations (2) and (3) shall apply to all the appointments by a CMI after these
regulations coming into force:
Provided that all the capital market intermediaries already registered with the Authority
under these regulations as on the date of these regulations coming into force shall ensure
that their principal officer and compliance officer meet the above requirements on or
before October 01, 2025 or any other date as may be specified by the Authority.
(5) A CMI shall ensure that its employees shall undergo such certification courses from
such institutions, as may be specified by the Authority.
(6) A CMI shall have adequate manpower commensurate with its business activities in
an IFSC.
(7) The principal officer shall be responsible for the overall operations undertaken by
the CMI and shall also ensure that other employees of the CMI comply with the
obligations under these regulations.
(8) Where an entity has multiple registrations under these regulations, the principal
officer shall be appointed/ designated for each such registration separately:
Provided that an entity with registration as a broker dealer, clearing member,
depository participant, investment adviser, research entity, custodian or registered
distributor may have the same person as principal officer for these activities: 6
Provided further that an entity undertaking multiple activities, as mentioned in the
above proviso, shall have a separate official as a vertical head for its distribution
business activities: 7
Provided further that an entity with registration as credit rating agency and ERDPP may
have the same person as principal officer for these activities.
(9) Where an entity has multiple registrations under these regulations, the entity may
have the same person as compliance officer for ensuring compliances with all the
applicable regulatory and legal requirements for its activities as capital market
intermediary in the IFSC.
Provided further that the Authority may review sub-regulations (8) and (9) based on
the size, scale and complexity of business activities of the intermediaries and may
specify revised norms in this regard.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 9, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Every CMI must have two named people based in IFSC — a principal officer (in overall charge of operations) and a separate compliance officer (responsible for following the rules). Both must meet set education and experience bars. On education, the rule now accepts a professional qualification or a post-graduate degree/diploma in a wide range of fields (finance, law, accountancy, management, commerce, economics, capital markets, banking, insurance, and — added 12 January 2026 — actuarial science, fintech, science, technology, engineering or mathematics), or a CFA/FRM; a plain graduate degree also works if the person has 5 years' financial-services experience (reduced from 10). On experience, the principal officer needs at least 3 years and the compliance officer at least 2 years in financial services (an ERDPP's principal officer needs only 1 year in ESG). One person can be the principal officer for several related registrations (the shareable list was widened in 2026), and one person can be the compliance officer across all of an entity's registrations. Existing CMIs were given until 1 October 2025 to bring their officers up to standard.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The 2026 amendments loosened three things at once: the eligible degree fields (STEM/fintech added), the experience-only route (10 years down to 5), and the list of activities that may share a single principal officer. Read the current provision, not older versions, when testing an appointment. The principal officer carries operational accountability for the whole CMI, including making sure other staff comply — this is not a titular role.
regulation_content.practical_point: Check each proposed officer against both the education and the experience limbs (they are cumulative in effect — a shortfall on one is not cured by the other, except through the graduate-plus-experience route). Where an entity holds multiple registrations, decide up front who can double up as principal or compliance officer under the widened provisos, and keep a separate vertical head for any distribution business where required.
regulation_content.example: A firm wants to appoint a STEM post-graduate with 4 years' experience as its principal officer. Since the 2026 amendment added STEM fields to the qualifying list, the degree now qualifies; with over 3 years' experience, the appointment meets Reg 9.
regulation_content.risk_point: The recurring gap is appointing an officer against the old (pre-2026) criteria, or treating the principal officer as a figurehead while operations are run by someone who does not meet the bar.
regulation_content.interview_point: A CMI holds registrations as a broker dealer, depository participant and research entity. Can one person be the principal officer for all three after the 2026 amendment?
regulation_content.important_numbers: Principal Officer: ≥3 years' experience; Compliance Officer: ≥2 years' experience; graduate + 5 years' experience route (reduced from 10 w.e.f. 12-Jan-2026); ERDPP Principal Officer: ≥1 year in ESG; existing PO/CO to comply by 01-Oct-2025
regulation_content.responsible_person: Board / governing body (appoints Principal Officer and Compliance Officer)
regulation_content.applicability: Entities seeking a certificate of registration as a capital market intermediary in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
10. Furnishing of Information
(1) The Authority may require the applicant to furnish any further information or
clarification regarding itself or nature of the capital market activities or any related
matter to consider the application for grant of a certificate of registration.
(2) If required by the Authority, the applicant shall appear before the Authority for
personal representation.
(3) If required, the Authority may undertake an inspection of the office of the applicant
before the grant of a certificate of registration.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 10, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: While your registration application is being considered, IFSCA has three tools it can use. It can ask you for more information or clarification about yourself or your activities; it can require you to appear before it in person to explain your case; and it can inspect your office before deciding whether to grant the certificate. These are pre-registration powers — they operate during the application stage, and how promptly and fully you respond shapes how smoothly the application moves.
regulation_content.practical_point: Keep your documentation, office set-up and key people ready to be produced or examined once you file, since any of the three steps can be triggered while the application is pending. Treat a request for further information as time-sensitive — delays here stall the grant.
regulation_content.risk_point: Slow or incomplete responses to the Authority's queries, or an office that is not actually functional when inspected, are what hold up (or sink) an application at this stage.
regulation_content.applicability: Entities seeking a certificate of registration as a capital market intermediary in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
11. Registration requirements
The Authority shall take into account all matters which it deems relevant for grant of
registration to a CMI including the following:
(a) the applicant or its principal officer and compliance officer have the specified
qualification and adequate work experience;
(b) the applicant has the necessary infrastructure like adequate office space,
equipment, communication facilities and manpower to effectively discharge its
activities;
(c) the applicant satisfies the eligibility criteria, net worth and fund allocation
requirements, if applicable, as specified in these regulations;
(d) the applicant has satisfactory financial credit worthiness; and
(e) the applicant and its principal officers, directors/ designated partners, key
managerial personnel and controlling shareholders are fit and proper persons.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 11, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: This lists what IFSCA weighs before granting registration — it will take into account all relevant matters, including whether the applicant and its principal and compliance officers have the required qualifications and experience, whether it has the necessary infrastructure (office space, equipment, communications, manpower), whether it meets the eligibility, net-worth and fund-allocation requirements, whether it is financially creditworthy, and whether the applicant and its key people are fit and proper. In effect, it draws together the tests in Regs 6 to 9 into the grant decision.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: This is the decision-stage checklist, so it repays reading alongside the individual requirement provisions it references — net worth (Reg 7), fit and proper (Reg 8) and officer qualifications (Reg 9). 'All matters which it deems relevant' also leaves the Authority room to look beyond the listed items.
regulation_content.applicability: Entities seeking a certificate of registration as a capital market intermediary in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.provision_heading: A CMI shall ensure that any change in registration status/any penal action taken by
regulation_content.regulation_text:
12. Grant of registration
(1) The Authority may, after considering the application and on being satisfied that the
applicant has complied with the conditions laid down in these regulations and is eligible
to act as a CMI, and upon receipt of registration fees, grant registration to the applicant
subject to the conditions as deemed fit.
(2) If the Authority is of the opinion that the registration cannot be granted, it shall
communicate the deficiencies to the Applicant giving it thirty days’ time to rectify them.
(3) If the Applicant fails to rectify such deficiencies to the satisfaction of the Authority
within the specified time, the Authority may refuse to grant registration and shall
communicate the same to the Applicant, giving reasons for such refusal:
Provided that no such refusal shall be made by the Authority without giving the
Applicant an opportunity to make written submissions on the grounds on which the
registration is proposed to be refused.
(4) The CMI shall comply with any other conditions as may be imposed by the
Authority as it deems fit in the interest of the investors or orderly development of the
securities market, in an IFSC.
(5) The registration granted to a CMI may be withdrawn by the Authority only after
giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 12, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Once satisfied that the applicant meets the conditions and the fee is paid, IFSCA grants registration, and it can attach conditions it thinks fit. If it is minded to refuse, it must first tell the applicant the deficiencies and give 30 days to fix them; only if they are not fixed to its satisfaction can it refuse — and even then it must give reasons and a chance to make written submissions first. A registration can later be withdrawn, but only after a reasonable hearing.
regulation_content.practical_point: If the Authority flags deficiencies, treat the 30-day cure window as the priority — a timely, complete rectification is the difference between grant and refusal. Preserve the right to written submissions before any refusal or withdrawal.
regulation_content.risk_point: Missing the 30-day rectification window, or failing to use the written-submission opportunity, converts a curable deficiency into an outright refusal.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Authority gives 30 days to rectify deficiencies before refusing registration
regulation_content.applicability: Entities seeking a certificate of registration as a capital market intermediary in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
13. Period of validity
The certificate of registration granted to a CMI shall be perpetual unless it is suspended or
cancelled by the Authority.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 13, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A CMI's certificate of registration is perpetual — it does not need periodic renewal and continues indefinitely, unless IFSCA suspends or cancels it. So there is no expiry date to diarise; the focus shifts entirely to staying compliant so the registration is not withdrawn.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Certificate of registration is perpetual unless suspended or cancelled
regulation_content.applicability: Entities seeking a certificate of registration as a capital market intermediary in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
14. Surrender of registrations
A CMI may file an application with the Authority for surrender of its registration:
Provided that a trading member or clearing member or depository participant shall make
such application through the recognised stock exchange or recognised clearing corporation
or recognised depository, as the case may be:
Explanation. - The voluntary surrender of certificate of registration shall be effective only
after its acceptance by the Authority.
CHAPTER III
GENERAL OBLIGATIONS AND RESPONSIBILITIES
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 14, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A CMI that no longer wishes to be registered can apply to surrender its registration. A trading member, clearing member or depository participant routes that application through its exchange, clearing corporation or depository. The surrender only takes effect once the Authority accepts it — you cannot simply walk away; the registration continues until acceptance.
regulation_content.applicability: Entities seeking a certificate of registration as a capital market intermediary in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
15. Code of Conduct
A CMI shall abide by the Code of Conduct as specified in Schedule II.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 15, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Every CMI must follow the Code of Conduct in Schedule II. Part A applies to all intermediaries; Part B adds category-specific rules for each type (broker dealers, rating agencies, custodians, and so on). The Code is not optional soft guidance — it is a binding obligation, and breaches of it are enforceable.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Because the substance lives in Schedule II, this short provision is really a pointer — read it with both parts of that Schedule. Conduct breaches are a frequent basis for action under Reg 41, so the Code carries real enforcement teeth.
regulation_content.related_provisions: Schedule II, Part A,Schedule II, Part B
regulation_content.applicability: All registered capital market intermediaries in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.provision_heading: A CMI shall have and employ effectively appropriate resources and procedures
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 16, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A CMI must keep a defined set of books and records in electronic, retrievable form for at least 8 years: balance sheet, profit and loss account and auditor's report for each period, a net-worth statement for each quarter, AML/CFT/KYC documentation, client account-opening records and powers of attorney, records of its capital-market activities, complaint and grievance records, and anything else the Authority specifies. The 8-year retention and the quarterly net-worth statement are the two hard, testable requirements here.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Owner: Compliance Officer. Preserve all listed records electronically for a minimum of 8 years; produce a net-worth statement every quarter; keep AML/KYC and client-onboarding documentation current and retrievable.
regulation_content.risk_point: On inspection, gaps in the 8-year electronic trail — missing quarterly net-worth statements or incomplete client-onboarding records — are among the first things examined.
regulation_content.interview_point: For how long, and in what form, must a CMI preserve its client account-opening records and quarterly net-worth statements?
regulation_content.important_numbers: Books, records and documents preserved in electronic retrieval form for a minimum of 8 years; net-worth statement maintained each quarter
regulation_content.compliance_frequency: Ongoing; net-worth statement each quarter; records preserved for 8 years
regulation_content.applicability: All registered capital market intermediaries in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
17. Information to the Authority
(1) A CMI shall furnish to the Authority any material change in the information or
particulars previously furnished along with the application, which has a bearing on the
certificate of registration granted to it.
(2) A CMI shall intimate to the Authority any change in principal officer, compliance
officer or key managerial personnel to the Authority, within 15 days of such change.
(3) A CMI shall furnish such reports, returns, statements and particulars, in such
manner, interval and form, as may be specified by the Authority.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 17, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Three reporting duties run to the Authority here. The CMI must report any material change to the information it gave in its application that affects its registration; it must intimate any change in its principal officer, compliance officer or key managerial personnel within 15 days; and it must file whatever reports, returns and statements the Authority specifies, in the form and at the intervals set. The 15-day clock on a change of key officers is the concrete deadline to manage.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Owner: Compliance Officer / Principal Officer. Trigger: any material change to application information, or a change in PO/CO/KMP. Deadline: PO/CO/KMP changes within 15 days; other filings as specified.
regulation_content.risk_point: A silent change of principal or compliance officer beyond 15 days is a straightforward, easily-detected breach.
regulation_content.important_numbers: Change in Principal Officer, Compliance Officer or KMP intimated to the Authority within 15 days
regulation_content.compliance_frequency: Event-based (PO/CO/KMP change within 15 days) and as specified
regulation_content.applicability: All registered capital market intermediaries in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
18. Redress of grievances
A CMI shall take adequate steps for redress of grievances of the investors in accordance
with the requirements as may be specified by the Authority.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 18, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A CMI must take adequate steps to redress investor grievances, in line with whatever requirements the Authority specifies. In practice this means having a working complaints and grievance-handling process; the detailed standard is set by the Authority's requirements rather than spelled out in the provision itself.
regulation_content.applicability: All registered capital market intermediaries in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
19. Dispute Resolution
A CMI shall take adequate steps to ensure that disputes between a CMI and its clients
and/or investors arising out of or in relation to the activities of the CMI in IFSC shall be
dealt with in accordance with the dispute resolution mechanism as may be specified by the
Authority.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 19, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Disputes between a CMI and its clients or investors — arising out of its IFSC activities — are handled through the dispute-resolution mechanism the Authority specifies. The provision points to that mechanism rather than prescribing the process itself, so the operative detail lives in the Authority's framework.
regulation_content.applicability: All registered capital market intermediaries in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.provision_heading: A CMI shall ensure that the compliance officer has adequate freedom and power
regulation_content.regulation_text:
20. Business Continuity Plan
(1) A CMI shall maintain a business continuity plan identifying procedures relating to
an emergency or significant business disruption, commensurate with its size, nature and
scale of business.
(2) A CMI shall update its business continuity plan in the event of any material change
to operations, structure, business, or location.
(3) A CMI shall conduct an annual review of its business continuity plan.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 20, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A CMI must maintain a business continuity plan — a written playbook for coping with an emergency or major disruption — sized to its business. It has to update the plan whenever there is a material change to its operations, structure, business or location, and review the plan at least once a year. The annual review is the recurring, diariseable obligation.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Owner: Principal Officer. Maintain a BCP proportionate to the business; update it on any material change; review it at least annually and keep evidence of that review.
regulation_content.compliance_frequency: Annual review of the business continuity plan
regulation_content.applicability: All registered capital market intermediaries in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
21. Cyber Security and Cyber Resilience
A CMI shall have robust cyber security and cyber resilience framework in accordance with
the requirements as may be specified by the Authority.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 21, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Cyber security and cyber resilience are a standalone obligation: the CMI must maintain a robust framework that meets the requirements the Authority specifies. The provision sets the duty at a high level and leaves the detailed standard to those specifications, so compliance is measured against what the Authority has specified.
regulation_content.applicability: All registered capital market intermediaries in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
22. Risk Management and Internal Controls
(1) A CMI shall have a sound risk management system for comprehensively managing
risks.
(2) A CMI shall have adequate internal procedures and controls, given the types of
business in which it engages (including any activities which have been outsourced) with
the aim of protecting the interests of clients and their assets and ensuring proper
management of risk.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 22, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A CMI must run a sound risk-management system and have internal procedures and controls suited to its business — including any activities it has outsourced — aimed at protecting clients and their assets and managing risk properly. It is a governance-and-controls obligation: the firm must be able to show its risk and control framework actually fits what it does.
regulation_content.applicability: All registered capital market intermediaries in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
23. Change in control
(1) Where a CMI is operating in the form of branch in an IFSC, it shall intimate the
Authority, and the market infrastructure institution of which it is a member (if
applicable), within fifteen days of any direct or indirect change in control of the
intermediary.
(2) Where a CMI is incorporated in an IFSC, it shall seek prior approval of the
Authority, in case of any direct or indirect change in control of the intermediary.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 23, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Change of control of a CMI is handled two different ways depending on its form. A CMI operating as a branch must intimate the Authority (and the market infrastructure institution it belongs to, if any) within 15 days of any direct or indirect change in control. A CMI incorporated in IFSC must instead get the Authority's prior approval before any such change. So a branch reports after the event; an incorporated entity must clear it before.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The split matters commercially: for an IFSC-incorporated CMI, a change of control cannot be closed first and notified later — prior approval is a condition, which affects deal timelines and conditionality. 'Control' takes its Reg 3 meaning (more than 50% of voting rights or the right to run the entity), so indirect upstream changes can trigger it too.
regulation_content.practical_point: Establish at the outset whether the CMI is a branch or IFSC-incorporated, because that decides whether a control change needs prior approval or only a 15-day intimation. For an incorporated CMI, build the prior-approval step into any transaction timeline and test for indirect (upstream) control changes, not just direct ones.
regulation_content.example: An overseas parent sells its majority stake, indirectly changing control of its IFSC-incorporated CMI subsidiary. Because the CMI is incorporated in IFSC, the Authority's prior approval is needed before the change — a post-closing intimation would not be enough.
regulation_content.risk_point: The classic error is treating an IFSC-incorporated CMI like a branch and merely intimating a completed control change instead of seeking prior approval.
regulation_content.interview_point: How does the change-in-control obligation differ between a CMI operating as a branch and one incorporated in IFSC?
regulation_content.important_numbers: Branch: change in control intimated within 15 days; entity incorporated in IFSC: prior approval of the Authority
regulation_content.compliance_frequency: Event-based (change in control): branch intimates within 15 days; IFSC entity takes prior approval
regulation_content.applicability: All registered capital market intermediaries in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
24. Payment of Fees
A CMI shall pay the fees pertaining to annual fees, turnover based fees and any other fees
specified by the Authority.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 24, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A CMI must pay the fees the Authority sets — annual fees, turnover-based fees and any other specified fees. It is a straightforward continuing obligation; the amounts and basis are fixed by the Authority.
regulation_content.compliance_frequency: Annual fees, turnover-based fees and other fees as specified
regulation_content.applicability: All registered capital market intermediaries in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
25. Annual Compliance Audit
(1) A CMI shall have an annual audit conducted in respect of compliance with these
regulations by a member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India or a member
of the Institute of Company Secretaries of India or a member of the Institute of Cost
Accountants of India or any person authorised to conduct audit in a Foreign Jurisdiction.
(2) A copy of such compliance audit report for a financial year shall be furnished to
the Authority by the 30th of September of such year:
Provided that a trading member, a clearing member and a depository participant shall
also file a copy of such report to the recognised stock exchange, recognised clearing
corporation and depository, as the case may be.
(3) A CMI shall have additional audits and submit such reports as may be specified by
the Authority from time to time.
CHAPTER IV
SPECIFIC OBLIGATIONS AND RESPONSIBILITES
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 25, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: Every CMI must have an annual audit of its compliance with these regulations, carried out by a member of the ICAI, ICSI or ICMAI (or a person authorised to audit in a Foreign Jurisdiction). The compliance audit report for a financial year must reach the Authority by 30 September of that year, and a trading member, clearing member or depository participant must also file it with its exchange, clearing corporation or depository. The Authority can require additional audits and reports.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Owner: Compliance Officer. Frequency: annual. Get the compliance audit done by a qualified professional and file the report with the Authority by 30 September (and with the relevant market infrastructure institution, for broker/clearing/DP).
regulation_content.example: A CMI with a 31 March year-end must have its compliance audit for that year completed and filed with the Authority by 30 September the same year — a six-month window from year-end.
regulation_content.risk_point: Missing the 30 September filing, or using an auditor who is not a member of one of the named professional bodies (or authorised abroad), are the two failures to guard against.
regulation_content.interview_point: Who may conduct a CMI's annual compliance audit, and by when must the report reach the Authority?
regulation_content.important_numbers: Compliance audit report furnished to the Authority by 30 September of each year
regulation_content.compliance_frequency: Annual (compliance audit report to the Authority by 30 September)
regulation_content.applicability: All registered capital market intermediaries in IFSC

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
26. Broker dealers and Clearing members
(1) A broker dealer shall ensure compliance with the applicable laws, including bye-
laws, rules and regulations specified by the recognised stock exchange.
(2) A clearing member shall ensure compliance with the applicable laws, including
bye-laws, rules and regulations specified by the recognised clearing corporation.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 26, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: This puts the primary conduct-and-compliance duty for the two trading-side intermediaries where it belongs. A broker dealer must comply with the applicable laws and the bye-laws, rules and regulations of the recognised stock exchange it operates on; a clearing member must do the same for its recognised clearing corporation. So beyond these IFSCA rules, each also answers to its exchange's or clearing corporation's rulebook.
regulation_content.applicability: Broker dealers and clearing members

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
27. Global Access
A CMI, including a broker dealer, desirous of dealing in securities in Foreign Jurisdictions
shall comply with the norms and requirements specified by the Authority.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 27, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A CMI — including a broker dealer — that wants to deal in securities in Foreign Jurisdictions ('Global Access') must follow the norms the Authority specifies for that. Until those norms are issued, Chapter V of the old 2021 regulations continues to apply for this purpose (see Reg 47), so there is a live transitional bridge here worth noting.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: This is one of the few places where the repealed 2021 regulations still operate — Reg 47's proviso keeps the old Chapter V alive for global-access dealing until the Reg 27 norms are notified. Check whether those norms have since been issued before advising on cross-border dealing.
regulation_content.applicability: Capital market intermediaries (including broker dealers) dealing in securities in Foreign Jurisdictions

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
28. Credit rating agencies
(1) A registered credit rating agency shall enter into a written agreement with each
client whose securities or other permitted financial products it proposes to rate, and
every such agreement shall include the right and liabilities of each party and fee to be
charged by such credit rating agency.
(2) The client shall provide all co-operation required for arriving at a true and accurate
rating of the securities or other permitted financial products by a registered credit rating
agency.
(3) A registered credit rating agency shall inform to the client the rating assigned to
the securities or other permitted financial products.
(4) A registered credit rating agency shall continuously monitor the rating of securities
or other permitted financial products and carry out periodic reviews of the rating, unless
the rating is withdrawn.
(5) A registered credit rating agency shall generally not withdraw a rating so long as
the obligations under the security /instrument/ facility rated by it are outstanding:
Provided that a registered credit rating agency may withdraw a rating in the following
situations:
(a) Where the entity whose security/instrument/facility is rated is wound up or
merged or amalgamated with another entity,
(b) In case of non-cooperation from the issuers, or non-payment of agreed fee,
(c) At the request of an issuer, except where such request might give rise to
avoiding an imminent rating change, or
(d) Where such credit rating agency is constrained from providing service due
to events beyond its control:
Provided further that the reason for withdrawal of rating shall be mentioned in the press
release issued by the registered credit rating agency withdrawing such rating.
(6) A registered credit rating agency shall disseminate information regarding change
in ratings promptly through press releases and simultaneously to the recognised stock
exchanges (if the securities or other permitted financial products are listed on a
recognised stock exchange in an IFSC).
(7) A registered credit rating agency shall make public the definitions of the concerned
rating, along with the symbol and also state that the ratings do not constitute
recommendations to buy, hold or sell any securities or other permitted financial
products.
(8) A registered credit rating agency shall make available to the general public, the
information relating to the rationale of the ratings, which shall cover an analysis of
various underlying factors.
(9) A registered credit rating agency shall specify the rating process and file a copy of
the same to the Authority for record.
(10) A registered credit rating agency shall have professional rating committees,
comprising members who are adequately qualified and knowledgeable to assign a
rating, and all rating decisions shall be taken by the said committee.
(11) A registered credit rating agency shall exercise due diligence to ensure that the
rating given by it is fair and appropriate.
(12) A registered credit rating agency shall not rate securities or other permitted
financial products issued by it or any of its group entity.
(13) A registered credit rating agency shall have appropriate procedures and systems for
preventing trading on the basis of unpublished price sensitive information obtained by
them in the course of any professional assignment.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 28, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: This is the conduct rulebook for a registered credit rating agency (CRA — a firm that grades how safely a borrower can repay). It must sign a written agreement with each rated client setting out rights, liabilities and fees; the client must cooperate; and the CRA must tell the client the rating assigned. It must monitor ratings continuously and review them periodically unless withdrawn, and generally cannot withdraw a rating while the rated obligation is still outstanding — except in defined situations (the entity is wound up, merged or amalgamated; non-cooperation or non-payment; the issuer's request, unless used to dodge an imminent downgrade; or events beyond its control), with the reason stated in a press release. Rating changes must be released promptly by press release and simultaneously to the exchange (if listed). The CRA must publish rating definitions and make clear ratings are not buy/hold/sell advice, disclose the rationale behind ratings, file its rating process with the Authority, use qualified rating committees for all rating decisions, exercise due diligence for fair ratings, never rate its own or a group entity's securities, and prevent trading on unpublished price-sensitive information it picks up.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: Two safeguards are the backbone: the no-self-rating rule (a CRA cannot rate itself or a group entity), which protects against the sharpest conflict, and the controlled-withdrawal rule, which stops a CRA quietly dropping a rating to avoid publishing a downgrade. The 'reason in the press release' requirement is what makes withdrawal transparent.
regulation_content.practical_point: Put the client rating agreement, the rating-committee process and the conflict walls in place before rating anything, and treat the withdrawal restrictions as a hard control — a withdrawal to avoid an imminent downgrade is specifically barred. Keep the filed rating process current with the Authority.
regulation_content.risk_point: Enforcement attention falls on self- or group-rating conflicts, withdrawals that look designed to avoid a downgrade, and delays in releasing rating changes to the market.
regulation_content.interview_point: In what situations may a registered CRA withdraw a rating while the rated obligation is still outstanding, and what must accompany the withdrawal?
regulation_content.compliance_frequency: Continuous monitoring of ratings; periodic reviews
regulation_content.applicability: Registered credit rating agencies

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
29. Custodians
(1) A custodian shall separate and segregate its custodian activities from all other
activities.
(2) A custodian shall have adequate mechanisms for reviewing, monitoring and
evaluating its controls, systems, procedures and safeguards.
(3) A custodian shall enter into an agreement with each client detailing various
circumstances relating to custody of the securities or other permitted financial products
or funds.
(4) A custodian shall have adequate internal controls to prevent any manipulation of
records and documents, and to protect the records from theft and natural hazard.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 29, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A custodian (a firm that safe-keeps clients' securities and assets) must ring-fence its custody business: keep custodian activities separate and segregated from everything else it does, run adequate systems to review, monitor and evaluate its controls, sign an agreement with each client covering the custody arrangements, and maintain strong internal controls to stop records being manipulated and to protect them from theft and natural hazards. The theme is segregation and safekeeping integrity.
regulation_content.practical_point: Evidence the operational and record-keeping separation of the custody business from other activities, and keep the client custody agreements and the anti-manipulation controls documented and testable.
regulation_content.applicability: Custodians

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 30, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: This is the duty-set for a registered debenture trustee (the party that safeguards bondholders' interests). It must sign a trustee agreement with the issuer before the debenture subscription list opens, and cannot act where it is an associate of the issuer or otherwise conflicted. Its core duties (Reg 30(3)) run to the debenture holders: accept and hold a sound trust deed, call for periodic and fund-utilisation reports (within 7 days of the issuer's board meeting or 45 days of the quarter, whichever is earlier), communicate defaults, appoint a nominee director on two consecutive interest defaults or a security/redemption default, remedy breaches, ensure security and reserves are in place and assets are sufficient and unencumbered, enforce the security, convene holder meetings, and inform the Authority immediately of any breach. Before creating a charge it must do independent due diligence that the security is clean or properly consented, and it cannot walk away from the assignment until a replacement trustee is appointed.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The two triggers that convert the trustee from monitor to actor are the reporting deadline (7 days/45 days, whichever is earlier) and the 'two consecutive defaults' point, at which it must put a nominee director on the issuer's board. The no-abandonment rule — it cannot relinquish until a successor is appointed — is what prevents bondholders being left unprotected.
regulation_content.practical_point: Confirm independence from the issuer before accepting the trusteeship, and diarise the report-collection deadline on the earlier of the two clocks. Track defaults so the nominee-director duty is triggered on time, and never resign without a replacement trustee in place.
regulation_content.risk_point: Inspection focuses on conflicts with the issuer, late or missed default communication and nominee-director appointment, and gaps in the pre-charge security due diligence.
regulation_content.interview_point: At what point must a debenture trustee appoint a nominee director on the issuer's board, and can it resign mid-issue?
regulation_content.important_numbers: Debenture trustee calls for reports within 7 days of the issuer's board meeting or within 45 days of the quarter, whichever earlier; appoints a nominee director on two consecutive defaults
regulation_content.compliance_frequency: Reports within 7 days of the issuer's board meeting or 45 days of the quarter, whichever earlier
regulation_content.applicability: Registered debenture trustees

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
31. Depository Participants
(1) A depository participant shall ensure compliance with the applicable laws,
including bye-laws, rules and regulations specified by the recognised depository.
(2) A depository participant shall ensure that separate accounts are opened in the name
of each of the beneficial owners and the securities of each beneficial owner shall be
segregated, and shall not be mixed up with the securities of other beneficial owners or
with the participant’s own securities.
(3) A depository participant shall have adequate mechanisms for the purpose of
reviewing, monitoring and evaluating its internal accounting controls and systems.
(4) Where the records are maintained in electronic form, a depository participant shall
ensure that the integrity of the data processing system is maintained at all times.
(5) A depository participant shall reconcile its records with the depository, on a daily
basis.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 31, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: A depository participant (the client-facing agent of a depository, holding investors' securities in electronic form) must comply with its recognised depository's bye-laws, rules and regulations, and must protect the integrity of clients' holdings: open a separate account for each beneficial owner and keep each owner's securities segregated from other owners' and from its own; maintain systems to review and monitor its internal accounting controls; preserve the integrity of its data processing where records are electronic; and reconcile its records with the depository every single day. The daily reconciliation and the strict segregation are the operational core.
regulation_content.compliance_point: Owner: the depository participant. Keep beneficial-owner accounts separate and segregated at all times; reconcile records with the depository daily; maintain electronic-data integrity controls.
regulation_content.risk_point: Any mixing of one client's securities with another's or with the participant's own holdings, and any lapse in the daily reconciliation, are serious and readily-detected breaches.
regulation_content.applicability: Depository participants

regulation_content.regulation_name: International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025
regulation_content.regulation_text:
32. Distributors
(1) A registered distributor may undertake the following activities:
(a) Distribution of capital market products and/or services to any client in IFSC or
Foreign Jurisdiction: The capital market products and/or services offered by any
regulated financial entity set up in India, IFSC, jurisdictions which are identified in
the notification published in the Gazette of India vide no. G.S.R. 882(E) dated
November 28, 2019, as may be revised from time to time, or any other jurisdiction
as may be specified by the Authority, may be distributed to any client in IFSC or
foreign jurisdictions;
(b) Distribution of capital market products and/or services to sophisticated
investors in IFSC or Foreign Jurisdictions: The capital market products and/or
services offered by any issuer or service provider, respectively, which is set up in
India, IFSC or any foreign jurisdiction may be distributed to sophisticated investors
in IFSC or foreign jurisdictions;
(c) Distribution of capital market products and/or services to any client in India:
The capital market products and/or services offered by any regulated financial entity
set up in IFSC, jurisdictions which are identified in the notification published in the
Gazette of India vide no. G.S.R. 882(E) dated November 28, 2019, as may be
revised from time to time, or any other jurisdiction as may be specified by the
Authority, may be distributed to any client in India;
(d) Distribution of capital market products and/or services to sophisticated
investors in India: The capital market products and/or services offered by any issuer
or service provider, respectively, which is set up in IFSC or any foreign jurisdiction,
may be distributed to sophisticated investors in India; and
(e) Any other activities as may be specified by the Authority.
Explanation: For the purpose of distribution activities under these regulations,
(a) “capital market products” shall mean “securities” as defined under sub-section
(h) under section 2 of Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956, and includes
similar instruments by whatever name called, issued or created by any issuer in
IFSC, India or Foreign Jurisdictions, and such other instruments as may be specified
by the Authority;
(b) “capital market products and services” shall collectively mean and include
capital market products and capital market services; and
(c) “capital market services” shall mean and include investment advisory services,
portfolio management services, by whatever name called, provided by a service
provider which is a regulated financial entity, and such other services as may be
specified by the Authority.
(2) For distribution of capital market products and/or services offered by a regulated
financial entity to all types of clients, the registered distributor shall ensure that such
products or services have been authorised, vetted or approved for offering to all types
of investors, by the relevant regulatory or supervisory authority of such regulated
financial entity:
Explanation: For the purpose of this regulation, “regulated financial entity” means an
issuer or a service provider set up in India, an IFSC or any Foreign Jurisdiction, which
is registered, authorised, licensed or regulated by any regulatory or supervisory
authority of its home jurisdiction for carrying out activities related to asset management,
funds management, investment advisory, portfolio management or any other similar
activity, by whatever name called.
(3) A registered distributor while undertaking various permissible activities shall
ensure compliance with all applicable laws as prevalent in the jurisdictions of issuers,
service providers and clients.
(4) A registered distributor shall comply with the requirements specified by the
Authority.
regulation_content.source_reference: Reg 32, International Financial Services Centres Authority (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 (IFSCA/GN/2025/003, as amended up to 12-Jan-2026)
regulation_content.simple_explanation: This maps out what a registered distributor (a firm that, for a fee or commission, markets capital-market products and services to clients) may do and on what terms. It sets out four permitted distribution channels — to any client in IFSC or a foreign jurisdiction, to sophisticated investors in IFSC or abroad, to any client in India, and to sophisticated investors in India — each keyed to where the product's issuer or service provider is set up and to the specified jurisdiction list. For products of a regulated financial entity offered to all types of clients, the distributor must ensure the product was authorised, vetted or approved for such investors by that entity's home regulator. Throughout, the distributor must comply with the laws of the issuers', service providers' and clients' jurisdictions. The definitions of 'capital market products' and 'services' and 'regulated financial entity' set the boundaries of what may be distributed and by whom.
regulation_content.regmate_comment: The channel rules turn on two variables — where the product originates and who the client is (all clients versus sophisticated investors only) — so the distributor must classify both before it distributes.
